title: Words, backgrounds and other tests
summary: Real memories store **words**, not single bits, and some faults need patterns that March tests alone do not create. This topic covers data backgrounds for word-oriented memories, the checkerboard and retention tests, and why tests that grow with N² are used only in the lab.
objectives: Apply a March test to a word-oriented memory with data backgrounds.
Compute the number of backgrounds log₂(B) + 1 for B-bit words.
Describe the checkerboard and retention tests and what they detect.
Explain why GALPAT and walking patterns are not used in production.

blocks.md:
In a memory with **B-bit words**, one address reads or writes B cells at once. A March test is applied to words by giving 0 and 1 a new meaning:

- **w0** → write a **data background** D (a B-bit pattern),
- **w1** → write its inverse **D̄**, and the reads compare with D or D̄.

Faults *between* words behave exactly as in a bit-oriented memory. But for **coupling faults inside one word** the aggressor and victim are written at the same time — with D = 00…0 they always get the same value. So the test is repeated with **several backgrounds**.

blocks.caption: Four backgrounds are enough for an 8-bit word
Backgrounds for intra-word coupling faults (N = number of words)

blocks.title: Logical is not physical
blocks.md: Neighbouring addresses are not always neighbouring rows, and the bits of a word are often spread over the array by **column multiplexing** (Topic 2 of *Memories and Their Faults*). Patterns that care about physical neighbours — like the checkerboard below — must use the memory's **address and data scrambling** information.

steps.title: Write and read the checkerboard
steps.md: Every cell gets the **opposite** value of its four physical neighbours. Then all cells are read.

steps.title: Write and read the inverse
steps.md: The same with every value inverted. Together: **4N** operations.

blocks.md:
The checkerboard puts the **largest possible difference** between neighbours. A short (bridge) between two neighbours, or leakage from one cell to the next, shows up as a wrong value. With a **pause** before each read it is also a simple retention test.

Its weakness: it makes few transitions and visits the addresses in only one order, so it misses most **address-decoder** and **transition** faults. In practice it is used **together with** a March test — often as an extra background for the March test itself.

blocks.title: The pause dominates
blocks.md: A 10N March test on a 1 Mi-word memory takes about 0.1 s at 100 MHz; two retention pauses of 100 ms add another 0.2 s. To save time, all memories of a chip pause **at the same time**, and the pause can overlap with other tests.

items.title: Walking 1 / walking 0
items.md: Fill the memory with 0. Write 1 into one cell, then **read all other cells** to check that none changed; restore the cell and move on to the next. Every cell is the aggressor once, and every other cell is checked each time → about **2N²** operations.

items.title: GALPAT (galloping pattern)
items.md: Like walking, but the reads **alternate** between the base cell and each other cell: read base, read cell j, read base, read cell k, … This also checks the read path between every pair of addresses → about **4N²** operations.

items.title: Butterfly and sliding diagonal
items.md: Variants that check only the neighbours of the base cell (or a diagonal) to cut the time — still longer than March tests and with less provable coverage.

columns: Time for 1 Mi words at 100 MHz
blocks.caption: Tests that grow with N² are far too slow for production

blocks.title: Where N² tests still live
blocks.md: On **small** memories, on a few chips in the lab for **characterisation**, or for **diagnosis** of a known bad block. March tests with the right elements catch the same fault models in linear time.

questions.text: How many data backgrounds are needed for intra-word coupling faults in a memory with 32-bit words?
When a March test is applied to a word-oriented memory with background D, what does **w1** mean?
Why does a single background D = 00…0 miss coupling faults inside one word?
options: Aggressor and victim in the same word are always written with the same value at the same time.

questions.text: What does the checkerboard test detect well? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Data-retention faults, when pauses are added

questions.text: What does **Del** mean in a March test?
options: A pause with no memory access, for retention faults

questions.text: GALPAT is the standard production test for large embedded memories.
